audit_scope.description: This batch covers EL-centric specifications (EVM interpreter, arithmetic opcodes, precompiles, transaction processing, BASEFEE opcode, SELFDESTRUCT, Constantinople fork activation, ENR discovery protocol, eth_symbol RPC) and one EL/CL cross-cutting spec (EIP-6110 on-chain validator deposits). The primary audit focus is EL state transitions and validation, with CL interaction at the deposit processing boundary.

out_of_scope: Beacon Chain state transitions beyond deposits

misclassified_entities.reason: Beneficiary address in SELFDESTRUCT is a passive recipient, not an entity that sends data into the system. It is an internal address target, not an external entity providing input.
Smart contract developer is a compile-time actor, not a runtime external entity interacting with the EVM. Developer input is mediated through compiled bytecode, not direct system interaction.
Calling contract/EOA initiating a CALL to a precompile is an internal EVM execution context, not an external entity. The actual external entity is the transaction sender who initiated the call chain.
Message caller within EVM is an internal execution context. The true external entity is the transaction originator (EOA) who submitted the transaction via RPC or P2P.
Transaction signer is the same entity as the transaction source (user). The signature is part of the transaction data, not a separate external entity.

trusted_external_entities.name: Peer Node via P2P Network
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: P2P devp2p protocol (block propagation, transaction relay, ENR discovery packets)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Peer nodes communicate over unauthenticated P2P network. Any node can join and send arbitrary data including malformed blocks, invalid transactions, and spoofed ENR records. Eclipse attacks and invalid block injection are archetypal threats.

trusted_external_entities.name: User via JSON-RPC
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: JSON-RPC API (eth_sendRawTransaction, eth_symbol, and other RPC methods)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Public JSON-RPC endpoints accept unauthenticated requests. Users can submit malformed transactions, oversized calldata, and resource-exhaustion payloads. Covers transaction sources (EXT-TX-SOURCE), contract callers (EXT-USER), wallet clients (EXT-WALLET-CLIENT), and stakers (EXT-STAKER) submitting deposit transactions.

trusted_external_entities.name: Block Producer (Miner/Validator) via P2P
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: P2P block propagation (new block headers and bodies)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Block producers submit blocks via P2P that must be fully validated. A malicious block producer could craft blocks with incorrect fork activation, invalid state transitions, or manipulated base fees. Block content is never trusted without validation.

trusted_external_entities.name: Untrusted Discovery Peer via UDP
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Discovery protocol UDP (ENRRequest/ENRResponse, Ping/Pong with enr-seq)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Discovery protocol peers are completely untrusted. They can send amplification attack packets, spoofed ENR records, and expired or malformed discovery messages. Prior ping exchange provides minimal authentication but no content trust.

trusted_external_entities.name: RPC Node Provider
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: JSON-RPC responses (eth_symbol and other informational endpoints)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: When a client connects to a third-party RPC node, the node operator can return arbitrary data. Malicious RPC nodes can deceive users about network identity (false currency symbols), provide incorrect chain data, or censor transactions. No cryptographic verification of informational responses exists.

trusted_external_entities.name: Attacker via Deposit Transaction Spam
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Deposit contract calls via eth_sendRawTransaction triggering DepositEvent logs
trusted_external_entities.rationale: An attacker can submit many deposit transactions to inflate block processing time via BLS signature verification at the consensus layer. While economically costly (~1000 ETH per second of delay), this is an identified DoS vector especially targeting optimistic sync nodes. Maximum 8192 deposits per payload could cause ~8 second processing delay.

trusted_external_entities.name: Consensus Layer via Engine API
trusted_external_entities.rationale: The CL communicates with EL over JWT-authenticated Engine API. The channel is authenticated but deposit request content forwarded from execution payloads must still be validated. EIP-6110 deposit data passes from EL logs through CL and back; each layer must validate independently.

trusted_external_entities.name: Malicious Validator via CL P2P
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: CL P2P gossip (beacon blocks with execution payloads containing deposit_requests)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Archetypal CL attack vector. A malicious validator can propose blocks with crafted execution payloads containing manipulated deposit data, attempt to exploit the Eth1Data deprecation transition, or submit conflicting attestations. All proposed data must be fully validated.

boundary_edges.security_assumption: Full block validation required: header fields, transaction validity, state transition correctness, fork-specific rule application (Constantinople, Cancun, Prague). Must verify block number against fork thresholds for correct ruleset selection.
Must validate prior ping exchange history to prevent amplification attacks. Must check expiration timestamp validity. Must not respond to ENRRequests from peers without recent ping exchange.

Must verify request-hash matches a pending ENRRequest. Must verify secp256k1 signature on the ENR record. Must not accept ENR records with invalid signatures or that do not correspond to a pending request.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Discovery protocol Ping/Pong with enr-seq field
boundary_edges.security_assumption: Must validate enr-seq field is a valid integer. Sequence number comparison is informational only; cached ENR outdated status should trigger ENRRequest but not automatically trust new data.

Full transaction validation required: signature recovery and verification (SECP256K1 r,s bounds, signing hash), type discrimination (legacy, EIP-2930, EIP-1559, EIP-4844), intrinsic gas calculation and sufficiency check, nonce overflow check (EIP-2681), init code size limit (EIP-3860), chain ID replay protection.

Read-only informational endpoint with no consensus implications. Response format must be valid JSON-RPC. No content validation possible for the symbol string itself. Clients should cross-reference with chain ID.

Clients must not rely solely on eth_symbol or other informational RPC responses for security-critical decisions. Wallets must cross-reference symbol with chain ID and other verifiable identifiers. Malicious nodes can return arbitrary symbol strings.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Deposit contract call via transaction execution
boundary_edges.security_assumption: Deposit contract address must be validated (DEPOSIT_CONTRACT_ADDRESS). Event signature must match DEPOSIT_EVENT_SIGNATURE_HASH. Deposit data must be exactly 576 bytes. Log parsing must maintain strict ordering. Gas cost per deposit provides economic protection but optimistic sync nodes face amplified processing overhead from BLS signature verification.

JWT authentication validates channel identity but deposit content must be independently validated. EL must verify deposit_requests match logs extracted from executed transactions. Mismatch between CL-provided deposits and EL-computed deposits must cause block rejection.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Beacon block with execution payload containing deposit_requests
boundary_edges.security_assumption: All deposits in execution payload must be validated by re-executing the block and comparing extracted deposit logs. Eth1Data deprecation transition must be handled correctly: deposit_requests_start_index alignment check must prevent double-processing of deposits during the legacy-to-onchain transition.

Block producers cannot bypass fork activation rules. Nodes must independently verify block number against network-specific fork thresholds (e.g., Constantinople mainnet=7,280,000). Incorrect fork block configuration leads to chain splits. All constituent EIPs must activate atomically.
